newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-NORMAN AND HOCH WIN SEMI-FINALS AT WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-NORMAN AND HOCH WIN SEMI-FINALS AT WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP.

text.p: Australian Greg Norman and American Scott Hoch won their semi-final matches at the $3.65 million Andersen Consulting World Championship of golf on Saturday.
Norman beat Japan's Hisayuki Sasaki 5 and 4, and Hoch dusted off Britain's Sam Torrance 4 and 2 in calm, cool conditions at Grayhawk.
Norman and Hoch will play over 36 holes in Sunday's final, worth $1 million to the winner, and Sasaki and Torrance will play-off for third.
"It was a good, solid performance," said Norman, who lost the first hole to Sasaki's birdie, but won the next four holes to take a commanding lead.
"I blocked a few drivers, but all-in-all I was hitting the ball crisply."
Asked whether his stature had intimidated Sasaki, Norman said: "I hope my seven birdies had more to do with with it than my stature. I know I didn't want to get beaten by him."
Norman, in typically swashbuckling style, ended the match by sinking a bunker shot from 20 feet for birdie at the par-five 14th.
"I missed many putts today," Sasaki said. "When I missed short putts on three and four it changed the flow of play."
Hoch, meanwhile, produced a superb performance, reeling off seven birdies and an eagle.
"It doesn't get a whole lot better," he said. "I only had one poor shot today. I was hitting my irons pretty straight and the right distance."
It took Hoch a while to shrug off Torrance, however.
Both players birdied the second and third holes, before Hoch eagled the par-four fourth with a six-iron from 172 yards.
Torrance birdied the next to make it all square again, and both players birdied the sixth.

Hoch birdied the seventh to go 1 up, which is how it remained until the pivotal par-four 10th hole. After yanking his drive, his only errant shot all day, Hoch chipped back to the fairway, 99 yards from the hole.
Torrance, meanwhile, was on the green in regulation, but Hoch hit a sand wedge to five feet and saved par, winning the hole after Torrance three-putted.
Suddenly two up, Hoch was never headed after that: "It was like running into a brick wall," said Torrance.
"Scott played great. The front nine we knocked the flag out every hole. The back nine was frustrating. Ten was a killer, because it looked like I was going to get back to all square."

Nine months after the championship started with 32 players divided into four regional brackets, the field has been whittled down to two survivors, the world's top-ranked player and an American who is playing as though he were number one.
